content.content:
=== homes.py
homes.py: where a status that an entry of POSITIONS.md states may already live.

    python3 -I homes.py 151            (or P-151)
    python3 -I homes.py 151 --top 8    candidates per sentence (default 5)
    python3 -I homes.py 151 --at REV   the three files as commit REV holds them

Splits the entry (the working tree's POSITIONS.md; for an entry struck from it, its text as it
last stood, said so at the top) into sentences, and a sentence into its clauses
at the semicolons outside parentheses; a clause keeps the label that opens its sentence, as
"Built:" or "Still to build:". A clause states a status when it, its label or its sentence holds
one of the status words: built, to build, landed, pending, default, waits, standing go, listed for his
review, open, held, parked, owed, taken, stands at, returns after, not moved, and the like.

For each such clause it lists the candidates that may already hold the same point: the numbered
items of review-queue.md's lists (b) and (c), and the lines of PLAN.md (a numbered sub-line also
carries its parent's item number, and its own number as a fork when the parent counts forks).
A candidate is listed when it names the entry or shares a distinctive term with the clause:
  row N, item N (PLAN's), review-queue item N, fork N, way N, batch N, rung X, phase N, ask N,
  decision X, another entry's P-N, a name in backticks (a commit hash too), a dotted finding
  name such as judge-review.1 or A.skeptic.2
Each shared term weighs by its rarity among the candidates (log of the candidates over those
holding it); naming the entry adds 2; content words shared (four letters or more, beyond common
words) add a little, to order near-ties, and are printed apart. Candidates are ranked by that
weight, and each is printed with what it shares, for the scout to confirm or reject.

=== later.py
later.py: his messages after an entry's creation that may bear on it, though no commit of the
entry followed them (his later word may have gone into a skill or another record instead).

    python3 -I later.py 148                   (or P-148)
    python3 -I later.py 148 --top 25          how many to print (default 15)
    python3 -I later.py 148 --at 36f7db77c --until 2026-10-21T20:54
                                              the entry's text at a commit, and no message after a time

The candidates are his messages in the coordinating sessions (tlib.COORDINATING) from the entry's
creation on (for an entry struck from POSITIONS.md, its last text is read, and the list runs on
past the removal) (the first commit of its trail that made its text), less those that leads.py already
printed near the entry's own commits. Each is scored by the entry's distinctive terms:
  - its title's words, beyond common words (a stop list, and words in more than a tenth of his
    messages), lightly stemmed (possessive and plural off, cut to 7 letters); each weighs its
    rarity in his messages, log(messages / messages holding it);
  - its names in backticks, weight 3 each.
A term in his own words (lines that do not start with ">") counts whole; a term only in the
exchange around his message (the coordinator's message he answered, by the reply chain, its
reply to him, and the lines he quoted) counts half. A message also gains 8 when it falls in the
30 minutes before a commit that changed a file the entry names in backticks (`compiler.md`), other
than the entry's own commits, in lines that hold a title term (3 when the lines hold none): that
is where his word may have gone. Naming the entry's number (P-148, or as dictated, P148) adds 8 in
his words, 2 in the exchange. A message is a candidate when its weight is at least 5 (MIN) and it
holds a term in his own words or falls before such a commit. Printed: rank, weight, time, whether it
is after the entry's last change, the terms (in parentheses when only in the exchange), the commit
it precedes, and its first 300 characters; then how many candidates there were in all.

=== pointers.py
pointers.py: every line of the record that names an entry of POSITIONS.md by its number.

    python3 -I pointers.py 86            (or P-86)
    python3 -I pointers.py 86 --at REV   the files as commit REV holds them

Searches, at the working tree: explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, POSITIONS.md, PLAN.md,
review-queue.md, HELD.md and BOOT.md; explorations/reviews/open-asks-*.md; and every file under
.claude/skills/. The history files (POSITIONS-history.md, FACTS-history.md) are not searched:
trail.py reads the first, and both only record. A line counts when it holds the number as a word:
P-86 matches, as in "P-86's" or "(P-86)", but P-860 and P-186 do not. A line that names a range
holding the number ("P-85 to P-88") is listed too, marked as a range.
Prints path:line and the line (cut at 400 characters around the number; --whole prints it whole),
grouped by file; the entry's own line in POSITIONS.md is marked.

=== comments.py
comments.py: his saved page comments that bear on an entry of POSITIONS.md.

    python3 -I comments.py 66            (or P-66)

He also comments on pages, and those comments are not in the transcripts. They are saved as
explorations/coordinator/positions-audit/evidence/curator-comments-*.md: a section per thread,
headed "## On <what it was anchored to>", with one bullet per comment, "- HH:MM: "words"".
A section counts when its heading, or a comment counts when its own words, either
  - name the entry's number, also as dictated: P-66, P66, PE66, P 66 (not P-660), or
  - quote its title: a quoted run ("..." or curly quotes) of at least three content words, at
    least 60 % of which are words of the entry's bold title (case, possessives and punctuation
    ignored).
A section that counts is printed whole, with its heading; a comment that counts in another
section is printed with that section's heading. Each with its file and line.

=== near.py
near.py: the curator's messages in a window before a UTC time, each with the coordinating
session's message that it answered, found along the transcript's reply chain.

    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z            window 60 minutes before the time
    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z 15m        or 2h, 1d
    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z 15m --cut 2000
                                                        cut each printed text at 2000 characters
                                                        (his and the coordinator's), saying so;
                                                        by default every text is printed whole

For each message of his: its time, source (main, s1, queued: see show.py), session, length and
full text. Then the message he answered: the coordinator's turn that his message follows on the
reply chain (tlib.py says how the chain is read), every text of that turn whole, each with its
time and the file and line it was read from (the first copy, when a resumed transcript replays
it). Before it, one line for each turn the chain passed over as not addressed to him (replies to
Stop-hook feedback, to an agent's message or hand-back, to a task notification or check-in, to a
system reminder), and for each text written after he sent his message; a passed-over turn that
answers a notification and ends with an ask to him (a question mark, "The ask", "I recommend",
"your yes", ...) is marked, and the newest such turn printed whole, since he may have answered
it. When he quotes lines ("> ..."), the text on the chain that holds them is named, and printed
whole if it is not the answer. After it, the last lines of the three turns to him further back
on the chain, for a message that answers an older question. A queued message (sent while a turn
ran) starts at its delivery into the turn; texts written after he sent it are not taken. A
message on no chain the index holds (a queued one never delivered) falls back to the time: the
coordinator's last text before it, passing over replies to Stop-hook feedback.

=== quote.py
quote.py: does the curator's message at a UTC time hold a quote word for word?

    python3 -I quote.py "QUOTE" 2026-09-26T10:21:32Z
    python3 -I quote.py "QUOTE" 2026-09-26T10:21        a prefix: every message of his in that minute

The time is a prefix of his message's timestamp, as show.py takes it (a trailing Z is dropped).
For each message of his at that time it prints one verdict:
  EXACT        the quote is a substring of the message as stored
  NORMALISED   a substring once both have every run of whitespace made one space, ends trimmed,
               and the curly apostrophe U+2019 made a straight one (nothing else is changed)
  NO MATCH     neither; it then prints the longest run of the quote's words that the
               message holds word for word (after the same normalising), for a reader to judge
With the match it prints the message's text around it.

=== trail.py
trail.py: the trail of one entry of POSITIONS.md, from the repository's history.

    python3 -I trail.py 86            (or P-86)
    python3 -I trail.py 86 --short    the commit list only, one line each
    python3 -I trail.py 86 --at REV   the record as commit REV holds it

### D23. The numerics plans, decisions 1 to 5 (2026-09-27)

- Decision 1, ranges over `ZZ32` alone: a call in a gap (the draft names no width, has two `ZZ64` examples), following the prelude (`CompilerLibrary.fsi:173-174`) and the JVM's array length. Consistent with his 2026-09-22 principle. Cost: a range over another integer type is a static error; the draft's ℤ factorial as a product over a range became a recurrence in the specification's text (`reviews/batch-7R-conformance.md:100`), a loss of one showcase of the notation, in the specification and not in the model.
- Decision 2, `extends Object` written on the result-only parameters, and Q1 the bound `Any`: **a call with an error in it.**
  - The written bound is the specification's own idiom (its examples write it; the library never does). It clears 340 errors by making the solver bind the parameter to `Bottom`, the type with no values, "harmless for natives whose bodies the switch-over replaces". `fail`'s body stays. Since rung B every value-position `fail("...")` in the library (`FortressLibrary.fss:1430`, `:1460`, `:1506`, `:2521` among them) compiles to a call whose result is carried as `java/lang/Object` and fails JVM verification at load ("Bad return type"); before it, under the bound `Any`, the checker refused those calls "without context", a compile-time error (row 447 and its later notes). A checker count was lowered by turning a refusal into a crash. The switch-over meets it. The 2012 Types chapter's word is that `Bottom` is uninhabited and inexpressible (`types.tick:184-195`), so an instance at `Bottom` is nothing the designers meant to run; the honest treatment of a call typed `Bottom` is the one the specification already gives a `throw` expression, which has that type. Section 6, item 2.
  - Q1, the implicit bound `Any` where the draft says `Object` (`trait-parameters.tex:49-50`): a departure, justified by the library's practice (it declares its element types unbounded and instantiates them at tuple types, which `Object` excludes) and by the 2012 Types chapter, where `Any` is the top and `Object` excludes arrows. But it is a specification sentence taken as a default inside another decision and listed (POSITIONS:121, :129); the overloading judgement had called it "a decision of his". Batch 7b's rung S will write it. He should say yes to it in so many words (section 6, item 3).
- Decision 3, the inference rule with the numeral switch as batch N: a call filling the gap the draft left empty, in the direction Welterweight names ("the most specific instantiation"). Right. Six gated gaps opened; one, row 508, is judged under D25.
- Decisions 4 and 5: process. Fine.

------
### 3. Is the implicit bound of an unbounded type parameter `Any`, as the library and walk take it, or `Object`, as the draft says? (Q1; before batch 7b's rung S)

- The draft says `Object` (`trait-parameters.tex:49-50`). The library declares its element types unbounded and instantiates them at tuples, which `Object` excludes; walk and the gate's count read `Any`; the compile path's desugarer writes `Object` (row 412). The 2012 Types chapter has `Any` as the top. Batch 7 took `Any` as a default inside decision 2 and listed it; the overloading judgement had called it your decision.
- Options:
  1. `Any`, stated in the text with a callout, the compile path's `Object` setting named as the divergence until the switch-over collapses it. Touches one sentence and the naked-`Any` overloading rule, which rung S must then state as the checker reads it. Costs nothing new.
  2. `Object`, the draft's word. Touches the library: 163 refusals, mostly tuple index types, and the arrays' element types. Costs a library sweep against the library's own practice.
- Recommendation: 1, said in so many words.

### 4. In which order does the checker try a call's candidates? (row 508, item 34; phase 3)

4. **Q1, the implicit bound `Any` (D23).** Right in substance, wrong in form: a specification sentence changed by a default inside another decision. On the path only through the text; batch 7b's rung S writes it. Needs his explicit yes.
- Tension 4, the implicit bound. Before batch 7b's rung S writes the sentence (item 3).

\seclabel{type-param}

\begin{Grammar}
\emph{StaticParam} &::=&
\emph{Id} \option{\emph{Extends}} \options{\KWD{absorbs} \KWD{unit}} \\
\end{Grammar}

Static parameters may include one or more type parameters.
Syntactically, a type parameter consists of an identifier followed by an
optional \KWD{extends} clause, followed by an optional
``\EXP{\KWD{absorbs}\;\;\KWD{unit}}'' clause (described in
\secref{absorbing-units}).
If a type parameter does not have an \KWD{extends} clause, it has an
implicit ``\EXP{\KWD{extends} \TYP{Any}}'' clause.
\revision{revival-bound}{The Working Draft of February 2011 gave such a type
parameter the implicit clause ``\EXP{\KWD{extends} \TYP{Object}}''.
\TYP{Any} holds every value, tuples and \TYP{()} among them, which \TYP{Object}

interpreter reads the bound so.

has an upper bound Any'' (Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu, POPL 2019).

declarations the bound \TYP{Object} (row~412 of the revival's gap ledger), a

\TYP{Any} is the top of the type hierarchy:
all types are subtypes of \TYP{Any}.
\TYP{BottomType} is the bottom of the type hierarchy:
all types are supertypes of \TYP{BottomType}.
For types $T$ and $U$,
we write $T \Ovrsubtype U$ when $T$ is a subtype of $U$,
and $T \strictsubtype U$ when $T \Ovrsubtype U$ and $T \neq U$;
in the latter case,
we say $T$ is a \emph{strict} subtype of $U$.
We also say that $T$ is a \emph{supertype} of $U$ if $U$ is a subtype of $T$.
Thus, in the execution of a
valid Fortress program, an expression's runtime type is always a subtype of
its static type.
We say that a value is \emph{an instance of} its runtime
type and of every supertype of its runtime type; immediate subtypes of
\TYP{Any} comprises of tuple types, arrow types, \TYP{()}, and \TYP{Object}.

The exclusion relation is a symmetric relation between two types
whose intersection is \TYP{BottomType}.

There's no experiment folder for it, and it didn't break anything. It was a measurement a review worker made on 09-17 in a throwaway copy of the repository, which wasn't kept. You can read it in `explorations/coordinator/batched-climb-review.md`, finding 2 (lines 19-37, commit `e93b20efb`). It found two things:

- **A copied cache counts as empty.** Fortress names each cache file with a hash of the source file's full path. A copy of the repository at another folder therefore finds nothing, and rebuilds the library from scratch in about 145 seconds.
- **A symlinked build is worse than slow.** Linking a worktree's build back to the main tree made the compiler silently read the main tree's files. An edit in the worktree could then be ignored.

Its conclusion was "copy the build, never symlink, and let each worktree rebuild its cache cold." It never tried translating the cache to the new path; it just stopped there.

Last night's exploration did that translation. A copy works when you rename the cache files to the new path's hash, rewrite the path inside them, and date them after the checkout. Fortress then accepts the copy and rebuilds nothing, in about 3 seconds instead of 145. That's in `explorations/coordinator/build-cache-exploration.md`, with the script in `explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh`. Batch 9 was the first batch to use it.

Not nine steps; it's a short ask. The nine steps are for unfamiliar ground where no rule of yours applies yet. Here both rules are already yours, and the three bounds were a stopgap that your later rule made obsolete.

**Q: Drop the `extends Object` bounds that batch 7 wrote on `fail`, `builtinPrimitive` and `List`'s empty comprehension?**

- **Why they were written.** Each of these three has a type parameter that only its return type mentions, as in `fail[\T\](s: String): T`. In batch 7 the checker couldn't solve such a parameter. Writing `T extends Object` made it fall back to `Bottom`, which cleared about 340 errors. You approved that on 09-27.
- **What changed.** On 09-29 you decided the paper's instance rule: a parameter nothing fixes takes its declared bound, never `Bottom`. Batch 8 built it. Now, with the bound written as `Object`, a call where nothing (`()`) is expected has no valid type, because `Object` excludes `()`. So 18 library sites are refused, among them `Writer`'s natives, which every `println` goes through. Those calls never worked before either: they compiled but failed when loaded. Nothing that ran is lost.
- **Without the written bound**, the default bound is `Any`, your decision from 09-26. `Any` includes `()`, so those calls type-check. The original team wrote none of these three bounds.

The options:
1. **Drop them.** Three declarations, each in its interface file and its implementation. It clears 18 of the 29 errors. The other 11 need a checker change already planned for a later rung: passing the expected type into an `if` without `else` and a few similar spots. The specification already asks for that.
2. **Keep them.** The 18 refusals stay on the way to the switch-over.

A yes to 1 puts the library back to the team's own declarations and goes into batch 10. A no keeps 18 refusals of the library's own `fail` and `builtinPrimitive`.

Recommendation: 1.

You're close. Three corrections, then why `Any` isn't just the status quo.

**`Any` and `Bottom` are opposite ends.**
- `Any` is the top: every type sits below it, and every value in Fortress belongs to it.
- `Bottom` is the bottom: it sits below every type and has no values at all. It's the type of an expression that never returns a value, such as `throw`.
- The question in item 3 is only about the top. When a generic declaration writes `[\T\]` with no bound, what may `T` be?

**What `Object` is in Fortress.** It isn't Scala's `object` keyword, although Fortress has a similar keyword:
- A Fortress `object` declaration makes values. Without parameters it's a singleton, like Scala's `object`. With parameters, like `object Just[\T\](x: T)`, it's a constructor, much like a Scala case class. So your memory connects the right things.
- The type `Object` is the supertype of every value those declarations make.
- There are no Java-style primitives at the language level. `ZZ32`, `RR64` and `String` are all under `Object`. The unboxed `double` is only how the compiler may store an `RR64`.

**What `Any` has that `Object` doesn't:** tuples like `(ZZ32, ZZ32)`, functions like `ZZ32 -> ZZ32`, and the empty tuple `()`. In Fortress these are not objects. The 2012 Types chapter says the same: `Any` is the top, and `Object` excludes function types.

**Why `Any` isn't just the status quo:**
- The library's own design needs it. A two-dimensional array is indexed by a pair: `Array[\RR64, (ZZ32, ZZ32)\]`. A list of pairs is `List[\(K, V)\]`. Under `Object`, every generic container instantiated at a tuple would be refused. That was measured at 163 refusals, most of them tuple index types, including the arrays microGPT uses.
- The draft's sentence saying `Object` dates from 2008 to 2010, before the library instantiated generics at tuples everywhere. The 2012 Types chapter makes `Any` the top.
- The compile path currently writes `Object` for an empty bound (row 412), which is why it refuses generics at tuple types today. That divergence goes away at the switch-over.

So the choice is between the draft's 2008 wording and what the library needs and the designers' later text says. Option 1 writes `Any` into the specification with a callout recording that the draft said `Object`.

1+51	If a type parameter does not have an \KWD{extends} clause, it has an
2+51	implicit ``\EXP{\KWD{extends} \TYP{Any}}'' clause.
3+51	\revision{revival-bound}{The Working Draft of February 2011 gave such a type
4+51	parameter the implicit clause ``\EXP{\KWD{extends} \TYP{Object}}''.
5+51	\TYP{Any} holds every value, tuples and \TYP{()} among them, which \TYP{Object}
6+51	does not (the team's later Types chapter, Luchangco, 2012); \library\ are
7+51	written under \TYP{Any}, instantiating such parameters at tuple types, and the
8+51	interpreter reads the bound so.
9+51	The type group's paper of 2019 says the same: ``By default, each type parameter
10+51	has an upper bound Any'' (Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu, POPL 2019).
11+51	The compiled path still gives such a type parameter of a program's own
12+51	declarations the bound \TYP{Object} (row~412 of the revival's gap ledger), a
13+51	divergence that lasts until the compiled path is switched over to the
14+51	interpreter's library.}
